name: Erik Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you tell me stays confidential; feel free to separate your work voice from your private view. Tell me about a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Erik, 43, and I’m a junior developer at a tech company that runs a fare and receipt app. I have a two-year college diploma and still need a senior person to check the trickier fare rules. Most days I trace a wrong receipt, fix a small piece of code, and test it against old trips. I use an AI helper now and then to explain an error log, but I check its answer against the actual trip record.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job mean for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Ana, handles payroll for a care home. We have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is typical, we have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some similar jobs nearby. I like a plan I can check against the bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau leaves us fixing real fare errors, with a little help reading logs. I would want a person to compare any suggested fix with the passenger’s receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel mostly steady about work, though the mortgage always makes me count our buffer. A wrong fare can cost us trust even if it never costs my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching old trip records to receipts and use AI only to explain confusing logs. I’d continue moving 180 each month into our emergency account while both salaries hold. In the first year I’d teach my younger colleague to check an AI explanation against the fare table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the mortgage, but I expect my hours and Ana’s payroll hours to hold. The AI part seems manageable in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which receipt mistake taught you the most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A passenger once paid twice because the app treated a transfer as a new ride. I found it by laying the two receipts side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a newer colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show my colleague the fare table first, then let the assistant explain the log. If the AI explanation disagrees with the receipt, the receipt wins.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people fixing fare errors with minor log help.
I would compare every suggested fix with a **passenger receipt**.
think: I expect our **paychecks** to hold, though the mortgage keeps me careful.
I worry a **wrong fare** could cost trust even without a job cut.
do: **Keep** matching trip records to receipts and checking AI log explanations.
**Transfer** 180 monthly into emergency savings while both salaries hold.
**Teach** a junior colleague to compare AI explanations with fare tables.
feel: **Uneasy** about the mortgage, with expected household hours stable.
S0.quote: If the AI explanation disagrees with the receipt, the receipt wins.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** remains tied to fare records and a known table.
The **three-month buffer** and two stable salaries help, but a mortgage keeps him alert.

steps.text: Keep matching old trip records to receipts and checking AI log explanations
Transfer 180 monthly to emergency savings while both salaries hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI write fare code and answer many passenger questions. I would ask for a joint staff review of errors before management shortens the release schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry junior fixes like mine will be handed to software, and Ana’s payroll checks may also be automated. Three months of savings is useful, but two screen-work jobs could empty it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d test the approved assistant against twelve old wrong-fare cases and keep a list of misses. I’d ask my senior colleague to train me on the fare rules I still confuse, using our paid learning hour. If management cuts junior posts in the first year, I’d attend the staff association meeting with Ana to compare both workplaces’ plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Our two jobs touch screen work, but we have a few months and some local options to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana each ask at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would ask whether payroll corrections still need a named approver. I would ask whether a passenger can reach a person when a fare is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the twelve cases to our manager and ask which mistakes count in the speed target. If the tool misses a transfer, I would keep that case out of the live rollout.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed fare code and passenger replies.
I would seek a **staff error review** before release targets tighten.
think: I fear **junior fixes** and payroll checks could both move to software.
Our **three-month buffer** may be short if both wages wobble.
do: **Test** the approved assistant against twelve old wrong-fare cases this month.
**Study** confusing fare rules during a paid hour with my senior colleague.
**Attend** the staff association if junior posts are cut in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about two screen-based incomes, with some time to adjust.
S1.quote: Three months of savings is useful, but two screen-work jobs could empty it.
fieldNote: He tests **twelve concrete cases** before accepting a faster release schedule.
Both **fare code and payroll** face thinking-task change, while his staff action waits on announced cuts.

steps.text: Test the approved assistant against twelve old wrong-fare cases
Study difficult fare rules with the senior developer during paid learning time
Attend the staff association if junior posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 can do our fare-code thinking work by 2028. Ana’s payroll thinking work faces the same date; hands-on robots arrive around 2031 and do not protect either desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my junior role to go, and I worry Ana could lose payroll hours too. Three months of expenses saved would disappear quickly under a mortgage if both paychecks stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask both employers for written staffing and severance terms now, then freeze the planned car upgrade and keep the cash. Ana and I would draw a three-month essentials budget. In the first year after 2028, if I lose my job, I’d apply to real local openings and seek income help we qualify for; I would not promise the children a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because the household could lose both screen-work incomes. A budget gives us an order for the bills, not a replacement paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which car cost goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first cut would be the car upgrade, not the old car’s safety repair. We need a way for Ana to get to work if her job remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you contact the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call the mortgage lender before a missed instalment and ask what hardship terms apply. I would not use our last savings to make a larger payment without knowing the terms.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach fare code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would stress **payroll work** faces the same 2028 thinking-AI change.
think: I expect my **junior post** could disappear along with Ana’s payroll hours.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot carry two lost wages and a mortgage for long.
do: **Delay** the planned car upgrade while keeping safety repairs funded.
**Write** a three-month essentials budget with Ana now.
**Apply** for real jobs and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible loss of both household incomes.
S2.quote: A budget gives us an order for the bills, not a replacement paycheck.
fieldNote: His **household exposure** is simultaneous in 2028 because both jobs are thinking work.
He preserves **car safety** and makes income help conditional on eligibility, with lender contact before arrears.

steps.text: Delay the planned car upgrade but pay for its safety repair
Apply for actual local vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Seek eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to make our fare checks clear and teachable. The thinking work in my code and Ana’s payroll changes in 2031; robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think both jobs are still exposed, but five years lets us build a larger cash buffer and test other duties while we earn. I do not know whether fare support or staff scheduling will still be paid work by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take the company’s free course on passenger dispute handling and practise one disputed fare each week with the support desk. I’d help Ana ask whether her employer offers paid scheduling cross-training; if it does not, we would use free material when she has time. In the first year after 2031, if my code work ends, I’d apply only for support roles that still have openings and pay enough for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to prepare than in the two-year picture. I would still worry about Ana’s income because payroll is also on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show a support skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d bring a disputed transfer receipt and explain the correction to a support colleague. If I cannot explain it without code jargon, I need more practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ana’s employer refuses training time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ana’s employer will not pay for cross-training, she would keep her hours and use free material if she has time. We would not pay tuition out of the mortgage reserve.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to make fare checks teachable.
I know **2034 robots** do not delay the thinking-work change for either of us.
think: I expect **both jobs** to remain exposed despite five years of warning.
I cannot assume **other duties** will still be paid in 2031.
do: **Complete** the free passenger-dispute course and practise one fare case weekly.
**Help** Ana request paid scheduling cross-training, using free material if refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying support openings if my code role ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about both incomes, with some time for learning and savings.
S3.quote: I do not know whether fare support or staff scheduling will still be paid work by 2031.
fieldNote: The **five-year window** lets both adults test adjacent duties while wages continue.
Their **training costs** stay conditional: free for him, employer-paid or free for Ana.

steps.text: Complete the free passenger-dispute course and practise one case weekly
Apply for existing support roles that pay the mortgage if dismissed after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to improve the fare app and learn other work. Thinking AI reaches code and payroll in 2036; robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect some pressure on our jobs, but I do not see our pay ending soon. We can build the reserve without betting on a course that may not lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing receipts with senior review and save 180 a month while both paychecks hold. I’d take the company’s free customer-support lessons one evening a month. In the first year after 2036, if code work has shrunk, I’d compare actual support vacancies and pay before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long term, but the mortgage and children feel manageable with both incomes now. I can move carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show progress during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the senior developer to check one receipt correction each month and explain any rule I missed. I want progress I can see on actual fares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana and I would review the mortgage buffer each school year when the children’s costs rise. We would not put an untested course on a credit card.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve fare work and learn.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code and payroll shift.
think: I expect **both paychecks** to hold for now despite future pressure.
I would build **cash savings** before paying for an uncertain course.
do: **Keep** fixing receipts with senior review and monthly feedback.
**Complete** free support lessons monthly, then compare real openings after 2036 if coding shrinks.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term work, with current bills manageable.
S4.quote: We would not put an untested course on a credit card.
fieldNote: He uses **slow, visible learning** on real fares while the household still earns.
The **mortgage buffer** and free lessons come before any move to another paid role.

steps.text: Keep fixing fare receipts with senior review and monthly feedback
Save 180 monthly while both paychecks hold
Compare actual support vacancies and pay if coding shrinks after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Ana’s payroll and my code could both be cut before we save more. Written notice from both employers, a clear lender process and income help we qualify for would help. I would need real openings, not a promise that support jobs are always there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when a passenger is charged twice and a machine says the fare is fine. A passenger charged twice still needs a person who can refund the money.

headlineQuote: A passenger charged twice still needs a person who can refund the money.
portrait: Erik is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and three months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** to explain logs, then checks suggestions against receipts and fare tables.
His partner’s **payroll work** faces thinking AI alongside his coding job, making two household incomes vulnerable.
He tests **old fare cases**, uses free training and seeks only real support openings that cover the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut both his code pay and his partner’s payroll hours.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, clear lender terms and eligible income help would support the family.
